name: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation
lead: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation uses a carbon dioxide laser to treat lines around the mouth. CO2 lasers emit at 10,600 nm, vaporise tissue and heat the deep dermis, which is thought to stimulate collagen and elastin production.[1]
Several trial registrations cover perioral wrinkles, including a completed fractional CO2 study of 35 participants, but no results are cited here.[2][3] Sources are limited, so the article is short.

paras: CO2 lasers were used early in laser resurfacing, developed in the 1990s.[1] They are used for deep wrinkles and sun damage and carry a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers; fractional systems are described as safer than older ones.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed fractional CO2 trial for perioral rhytides (35 participants)[2] and a completed laser spot treatment trial (30 participants)[3]; a trial of a 2910 nm laser for perioral lines is recruiting.[4] Results are not summarised here. Separate physiology studies used CO2 laser pulses around the mouth to study pain reflexes, not rejuvenation.[5]

card.summary: Clinic laser resurfacing for lip lines; established technique with registered trials, but downtime and scarring risks apply.
card.note: Higher hypopigmentation and scarring risk than erbium lasers.

quick.overview:
A clinician uses a CO2 laser to resurface skin around the mouth to soften lines.

Trials are registered, but this article does not summarise results.
quick.mechanism: The laser vaporises thin skin layers and heats the dermis, prompting collagen remodelling.
quick.risks: Described risks include hypopigmentation, scarring and herpes outbreaks.
